title: Regulatory Risk Tiers
blurb: The EU AI Act's pyramid, plus the GPAI systemic-risk threshold. Sort each system into its tier.
source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act) Arts. 5, 6, 50, 51 and Annex III
hint: Drag each system onto its risk tier. Tier follows purpose and context, not how sophisticated the model is.
note: The tiers attach to the use, not the technology. The same model can be prohibited in one deployment, high-risk in another and minimal in a third.

zones.name: Unacceptable
zones.def: Prohibited practices under Art. 5. Not a risk to be mitigated — the practice may not be placed on the market or used at all.

zones.name: High risk
zones.def: Art. 6 and Annex III, or a safety component of a regulated product. Permitted subject to substantial obligations before and after placing on the market.

zones.name: Limited / transparency
zones.def: Art. 50 transparency duties: tell people they are dealing with AI, or that content is synthetic.

zones.name: Minimal
zones.def: Everything else. No obligations under the Act beyond those that apply to any software; voluntary codes may apply.

zones.name: GPAI with systemic risk
zones.def: General-purpose models meeting the Art. 51 threshold, with model-level obligations distinct from the use-based pyramid.

items.label: A government scheme scoring citizens' trustworthiness from unrelated social behaviour and using it to deny access to public services.
items.why: Social scoring by or on behalf of public authorities leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts is prohibited outright under Art. 5.

items.label: A system inferring employees' emotions from facial expressions during their working day, outside any medical or safety purpose.
items.why: Emotion inference in the workplace and in education is prohibited, with narrow medical and safety exceptions. This is why the ban catches HR analytics products.

items.label: A tool that scrapes facial images from the internet and CCTV indiscriminately to build a facial recognition database.
items.why: Untargeted scraping to build facial recognition databases is expressly prohibited, regardless of the operator's purpose.

items.label: A system using subliminal techniques beyond a person's awareness to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm.
items.why: Manipulative and exploitative techniques causing significant harm are prohibited. The test is material distortion of behaviour, not the technique's sophistication.

items.label: A CV-screening system that filters and ranks applicants for a role.
items.why: Employment and worker management is an Annex III area. Recruitment screening is the canonical high-risk example and attracts the full obligation set.

items.label: A model used by a bank to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons.
items.why: Creditworthiness assessment of natural persons is listed in Annex III, with a carve-out for detecting financial fraud.

items.label: An AI component that controls the safety function of a medical device already regulated under EU harmonisation law.
items.why: This is the Art. 6(1) route: a safety component of a product covered by listed harmonisation legislation and requiring third-party conformity assessment.

items.label: A system used to determine access to, or assign people to, educational institutions.
items.why: Education and vocational training decisions affecting a person's access are Annex III. The harm is to life chances, which is why the tier is high rather than limited.

items.label: A customer service chatbot that must make clear to the user that they are interacting with an AI system.
items.why: Art. 50 transparency: a person must know they are dealing with a machine unless it is obvious. That disclosure is the whole obligation.

items.label: An image generator whose synthetic outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated.
items.why: Marking synthetic content is an Art. 50 duty on providers of generative systems, independent of whatever tier the deployment sits in.

items.label: A deepfake published as part of a news item, which must be disclosed as artificially generated or manipulated.
items.why: Deepfake disclosure is a transparency obligation on deployers, with adjustments for evidently artistic or satirical work.

items.label: An emotion recognition system used outside a prohibited context, whose subjects must be informed of its operation.
items.why: Where emotion recognition is not banned outright, informing exposed people is an Art. 50 duty. The same technology sits in two different tiers depending on the setting.

items.label: A spam filter classifying inbound email for an enterprise mail service.
items.why: Spam filtering is the Act's own example of minimal risk. No obligations attach beyond general law.

items.label: An AI opponent controlling non-player characters in a video game.
items.why: Entertainment uses with no effect on rights, safety or access to services fall outside the tiers that carry duties.

items.label: An inventory forecasting model predicting warehouse stock levels with no effect on individuals.
items.why: No listed area, no safety component, no interaction with a person. Operational analytics is where most enterprise AI actually sits.

items.label: A model that optimises energy use in a data centre's cooling system.
items.why: Industrial optimisation touching no Annex III area and no person is minimal risk, however consequential it is commercially.

items.label: A general-purpose model presumed to carry systemic risk because its training compute exceeds the threshold set in the Act.
items.why: Art. 51 sets a compute-based presumption. This is a model-level classification and sits outside the use-based pyramid entirely.

items.label: A general-purpose model designated by the Commission as having high-impact capabilities equivalent to the most advanced models.
items.why: Designation is the second route into systemic risk, alongside the compute presumption. Either route triggers the same obligations.

items.label: A provider required to perform model evaluations, adversarial testing, and to track and report serious incidents at the model level.
items.why: Evaluation, adversarial testing, systemic risk mitigation and incident reporting are the Art. 55 obligations that only systemic-risk GPAI carries.

items.label: A provider required to ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.
items.why: Model-level cybersecurity is a systemic-risk GPAI duty. Baseline GPAI obligations — documentation, copyright policy, training-data summary — apply without it.
